claim: Gliomas are highly malignant brain tumors with poor prognosis and short survival.
source: Gliomas are highly malignant brain tumors with poor prognosis and short survival.
evidence: This is a general statement about gliomas that is part of established medical knowledge in the field.

claim: NAD+ has been shown to impact multiple processes that are dysregulated in cancer.
source: NAD+ has been shown to impact multiple processes that are dysregulated in cancer
evidence: This statement references established scientific knowledge about NAD+ and cancer, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Overexpressing enzymatically active NMNAT significantly promotes glial neoplasia growth in Drosophila.
source: Overexpressing enzymatically active NMNAT significantly promotes glial neoplasia growth and reduces animal viability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 2.

claim: Overexpressing enzymatically active NMNAT reduces animal viability.
source: Overexpressing enzymatically active NMNAT significantly promotes glial neoplasia growth and reduces animal viability.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: NMNAT interferes with DNA damage-p53-caspase-3 apoptosis signaling pathway by enhancing NAD+-dependent posttranslational modifications poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation (PARylation) and deacetylation of p53.
source: Mechanistic analysis suggests that NMNAT interferes with DNA damage-p53-caspase-3 apoptosis signaling pathway by enhancing NAD+-dependent posttranslational modifications (PTMs) poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation (PARylation) and deacetylation of p53.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 9 and 10, including immunoprecipitation and Western blot analyses.

claim: PARylation and deacetylation reduce p53 pro-apoptotic activity.
source: Since PARylation and deacetylation reduce p53 pro-apoptotic activity, modulating p53 PTMs could be a key mechanism by which NMNAT promotes glioma growth.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from prior literature about p53 modifications.

claim: Modulating p53 PTMs could be a key mechanism by which NMNAT promotes glioma growth.
source: Since PARylation and deacetylation reduce p53 pro-apoptotic activity, modulating p53 PTMs could be a key mechanism by which NMNAT promotes glioma growth.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and established knowledge about p53 modifications.

claim: NMNAT forms a protein complex with p53 and NAD+-dependent PTM enzymes.
source: Our findings reveal a novel tumorigenic mechanism involving protein complex formation of p53 with NAD+ synthetic enzyme NMNAT and NAD+-dependent PTM enzymes that regulates glioma growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9C and immunofluorescence colocalization studies.

claim: Glioma is the most common intrinsic tumor of the central nervous system (CNS).
source: Glioma is the most common intrinsic tumor of the central nervous system (CNS) and derives from the neoplastic glial cells or neuroglia (Goodenberger and Jenkins, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Goodenberger and Jenkins, 2012.

claim: Gliomas derive from neoplastic glial cells or neuroglia.
source: Glioma is the most common intrinsic tumor of the central nervous system (CNS) and derives from the neoplastic glial cells or neuroglia (Goodenberger and Jenkins, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Goodenberger and Jenkins, 2012.

claim: High-grade gliomas generally have a much poorer prognosis than lower-grade gliomas.
source: Based on pathological criteria, gliomas are classified from WHO grade I to IV, among which the high-grade gliomas generally have a much poorer prognosis (Wesseling and Capper, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wesseling and Capper, 2018.

claim: Several major cellular signaling pathways associated with glioma include RTK/Ras/PI3K, p53, and RB signaling pathways.
source: Several major cellular signaling pathways associated with glioma have been well studied, including RTK/Ras/PI3K, p53, and RB signaling pathways (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2008.

claim: IDH1/2 metabolism factors play important roles in glioma.
source: In addition, metabolism factors, such as IDH1/2, were found to play important roles in glioma (Yan et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yan et al., 2009.

claim: IDH1 is an enzyme of tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle in glucose metabolism and the main producer of NADPH.
source: IDH1 is an enzyme of tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle in glucose metabolism and the main producer of NADPH (Molenaar et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Molenaar et al., 2014.

claim: Drugs targeting glioma pathways showed a limited clinical response.
source: However, drugs targeting these pathways showed a limited clinical response, indicating a critical need for the mechanistic understanding of the metabolic requirement for glioma tumorigenesis.
evidence: This statement is based on general knowledge of clinical outcomes in glioma treatment.

claim: NAD+ is an essential signaling cofactor that regulates cancer metabolism through its co-enzymatic function for many bioenergetic pathways, including glycolysis, TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) is an essential signaling cofactor that regulates cancer metabolism through its co-enzymatic function for many bioenergetic pathways, including glycolysis, TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011.

claim: Multiple processes associated with NAD+ signaling are dysregulated in cancer, including DNA repair, cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis.
source: Multiple processes associated with NAD+ signaling are dysregulated in cancer, including DNA repair, cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis (Chiarugi et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chiarugi et al., 2012.

claim: Inherited polymorphisms and epigenetic repression of DNA damage repair genes are significantly correlated with the risk of gliomas.
source: Inherited polymorphisms and epigenetic repression of DNA damage repair genes are significantly correlated with the risk of gliomas, indicating that abnormal DNA damage repair plays important roles in glioma formation and progression (Chen et al., 2010; Qi et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2010 and Qi et al., 2017.

claim: PARP-mediated poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation (PARylation) is one of the key initiation events of DNA damage response and the main process that consumes nuclear NAD+.
source: One of the key initiation events of DNA damage response is poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP)-mediated poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation (PARylation), the main process that consumes nuclear NAD+ (Amé et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Amé et al., 2004.

claim: NAD+-dependent SIRTs-mediated deacetylation regulates many oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes in cancer cells.
source: Moreover, NAD+-dependent SIRTs-mediated deacetylation regulates many oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes in cancer cells (Brooks and Gu, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Brooks and Gu, 2009.

claim: A high level of NAD+ is observed in gliomas.
source: Consistently, a high level of NAD+ is observed in gliomas (Reddy et al., 2008; Tso et al., 2006), and 90% of gliomas are susceptible to NAD+ depletion (Tateishi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Reddy et al., 2008 and Tso et al., 2006.

claim: 90% of gliomas are susceptible to NAD+ depletion.
source: Consistently, a high level of NAD+ is observed in gliomas (Reddy et al., 2008; Tso et al., 2006), and 90% of gliomas are susceptible to NAD+ depletion (Tateishi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tateishi et al., 2015.

claim: NAMPT is the rate-limiting enzyme of the NAD+ salvage pathway.
source: In the past years, targeting NAD+ metabolism has been considered for cancer therapy, and most efforts have been focused on nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), the rate-limiting enzyme of the NAD+ salvage pathway, whose expression is increased in multiple types of cancer (Garten et al., 2015; Lucena-Cacace et al., 2018; Ohanna et al., 2018; Pylaeva et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple papers (Garten et al., 2015; Lucena-Cacace et al., 2018; Ohanna et al., 2018; Pylaeva et al., 2019).

claim: NAMPT expression is increased in multiple types of cancer.
source: In the past years, targeting NAD+ metabolism has been considered for cancer therapy, and most efforts have been focused on nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), the rate-limiting enzyme of the NAD+ salvage pathway, whose expression is increased in multiple types of cancer (Garten et al., 2015; Lucena-Cacace et al., 2018; Ohanna et al., 2018; Pylaeva et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple papers (Garten et al., 2015; Lucena-Cacace et al., 2018; Ohanna et al., 2018; Pylaeva et al., 2019).

claim: Several clinical trials of NAMPT inhibitors have failed due to low efficacy and high toxicities.
source: Disappointingly, several clinical trials of NAMPT inhibitors have failed due to low efficacy and high toxicities (Sampath et al., 2015), which demands the urgent consideration of an alternative target in the NAD+ metabolic pathway.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sampath et al., 2015.

claim: NMNAT is the last enzyme in the NAD+ salvage synthetic pathway.
source: Nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferase (NMNAT), the last enzyme in the NAD+ salvage synthetic pathway, has recently emerged as a potential candidate (Chiarugi et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chiarugi et al., 2012.

claim: NMNAT has three isoforms in mammals with distinct subcellular localizations: NMNAT1 in the nucleus, NMNAT2 in the cytosol, and NMNAT3 in the mitochondria.
source: NMNAT has three isoforms in mammals with distinct subcellular localizations: NMNAT1, in the nucleus; NMNAT2, in the cytosol; and NMNAT3, in the mitochondria (Berger et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Berger et al., 2005.

claim: NMNAT1 is considered a poor prognostic marker for renal cancer.
source: For example, NMNAT1 is considered a poor prognostic marker for renal cancer (Uhlén et al., 2015; Uhlen et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Uhlén et al., 2015 and Uhlen et al., 2017.

claim: Decreased NMNAT1 expression leads to epigenetic silencing of tumor suppressor genes.
source: Decreased NMNAT1 expression leads to epigenetic silencing of tumor suppressor genes (Henderson et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Henderson et al., 2017.

claim: Inhibition of NMNAT1 delays DNA repair and increases rRNA transcription.
source: Inhibition of NMNAT1 delays DNA repair and increases rRNA transcription (Song et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Song et al., 2013.

claim: In colorectal cancer, NMNAT2 upregulation correlates with the cancer invasive depth and TNM stage.
source: In colorectal cancer, NMNAT2 upregulation correlates with the cancer invasive depth and TNM stage (Cui et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2016 and Qi et al., 2018.

claim: In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), NMNAT2 enzymatic activity is upregulated by SIRT3-mediated deacetylation process or p53 signaling.
source: In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), NMNAT2 enzymatic activity is upregulated by SIRT3-mediated deacetylation process or p53 signaling (Li et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Li et al., 2013 and Pan et al., 2014.

claim: The depletion of NMNAT2 inhibits cell growth indirectly by reducing glucose availability in neuroblastoma cells.
source: Moreover, the depletion of NMNAT2 inhibits cell growth indirectly by reducing glucose availability in neuroblastoma cells (Ryu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ryu et al., 2018.

claim: The Ras/Raf/ERK signaling cascade is one of the most conserved pathways both in Drosophila and human.
source: The Ras/Raf/ERK signaling cascade is one of the most conserved pathways both in Drosophila and human, and a major component of the MAP kinase signaling stress-response network (Morrison, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Morrison, 2012.

claim: RAS mutations are the most commonly found oncogenic alteration in human cancers, most frequently observed in KRAS (85%), and to a lesser degree in NRAS (12%) and HRAS (3%).
source: RAS mutations are the most commonly found oncogenic alteration in human cancers, most frequently observed in KRAS (85%), and to a lesser degree in NRAS (12%) and HRAS (3%) (Simanshu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Simanshu et al., 2017.

claim: Upregulated RAS and mutant RAS have been detected in gliomas.
source: Upregulated RAS and mutant RAS have been detected in gliomas (Arvanitis et al., 1991; Guha et al., 1997; Knobbe et al., 2004; Rajasekhar et al., 2003), and activation of Ras has been used to model human glioma in Drosophila (Read, 2011; Read et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Arvanitis et al., 1991; Guha et al., 1997; Knobbe et al., 2004; Rajasekhar et al., 2003.

claim: Activation of Ras has been used to model human glioma in Drosophila.
source: Upregulated RAS and mutant RAS have been detected in gliomas (Arvanitis et al., 1991; Guha et al., 1997; Knobbe et al., 2004; Rajasekhar et al., 2003), and activation of Ras has been used to model human glioma in Drosophila (Read, 2011; Read et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Read, 2011 and Read et al., 2009.

claim: The constitutively active Ras85D mutation (G12V), Rasv12, has been suggested to be analogous to human oncogenic RAS mutation and used to induce tumor.
source: The constitutively active Ras85D mutation (G12V), Rasv12, has been suggested to be analogous to human oncogenic RAS mutation and used to induce tumor (Barbacid, 1987; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Barbacid, 1987 and Wu et al., 2010.

claim: Endogenous NMNAT is significantly increased in glial cells at both 100 and 150 hr AEL in Rasv12-induced glial neoplasia.
source: Notably, compared with the normal brain (Figure 1C and E), we found significantly increased endogenous NMNAT in glial cells at both 100 and 150 hr AEL.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C-F and quantified in Figure 1I-J.

claim: NMNAT was most prominently increased in the nuclear region in Rasv12-induced glial neoplasia.
source: NMNAT was most prominently increased in the nuclear region (Figure 1D and F), suggesting a possible role for NMNAT1, the nuclear isoform, in Rasv12-induced glial neoplasia formation in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: Knocking down Nmnat drastically reduced both the volume and the number of individual Rasv12-expressing glial cells in the brain and VNC at 100 hr AEL.
source: Interestingly, knocking down Nmnat drastically reduced both the volume and the number of individual Rasv12-expressing glial cells in the brain and VNC at 100 hr AEL (Figure 2A, C and D), demonstrating a strong antitumor effect of NMNAT inhibition in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, C, and D.

claim: NMNAT RNAi-mediated knockdown in normal glial cells (without Rasv12 expression) showed no growth inhibition.
source: We further analyzed RNAi-mediated knockdown of NMNAT in normal glial cells (without Rasv12 expression) and found no growth inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting NMNAT is not essential for normal cell survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of Nmnat-PC (nuclear), but not Nmnat-PD (cytoplasmic), significantly increased the total volumes of glial neoplasia.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of Nmnat-PC (nuclear), but not Nmnat-PD (cytoplasmic), significantly increased the total volumes of glial neoplasia (Figure 2B and C), while the number of glial neoplasia showed no significant difference among the groups (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Overexpression of Nmnat-PC (nuclear) significantly increased the lethality of flies.
source: The lethality of the flies (Figure 2E) was positively correlated with glial neoplasia size and overexpression of Nmnat-PC (nuclear) significantly increased the lethality.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Nmnat-PCWR (nuclear) overexpression did not significantly affect glial neoplasia volumes or numbers or survival outcome when compared to the control.
source: We found that Nmnat-PCWR (nuclear) overexpression did not significantly affect glial neoplasia volumes or numbers or survival outcome when compared to the control (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Nuclear enzymatically active NMNAT promoted glial neoplasia growth.
source: These results suggest that nuclear enzymatically active NMNAT promoted glial neoplasia growth.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing active and inactive NMNAT isoforms.

claim: NMNAT1 and NMNAT2 are increased in both glioma cells T98G and U87MG compared to SVG p12 cells.
source: Compared to SVG p12 cells, NMNAT1 and NMNAT2 are increased in both glioma cells T98G and U87MG (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: T98G cell proliferation was drastically inhibited when either NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 was knocked down.
source: Interestingly, we found T98G cell proliferation was drastically inhibited when either NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 was knocked down (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by xCELLigence real-time cell analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 knockdown reduced T98G cell proliferation as confirmed by MTT assay.
source: This observation was confirmed and extended in an MTT assay (van Meerloo et al., 2011), where NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 knockdown reduced cell proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by MTT assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpressing NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 promoted T98G cell growth.
source: In contrast, overexpressing NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 promoted cell growth (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by xCELLigence real-time cell analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Knockdown of NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 reduced the colony numbers of T98G cells.
source: Moreover, we used a plate colony formation assay to determine clonogenic survival (Franken et al., 2006), and found that knockdown of NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 reduced the colony numbers of T98G, while overexpression of NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 increased colony formation (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Overexpression of NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 increased colony formation of T98G cells.
source: Moreover, we used a plate colony formation assay to determine clonogenic survival (Franken et al., 2006), and found that knockdown of NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 reduced the colony numbers of T98G, while overexpression of NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 increased colony formation (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Knockdown of NMNAT significantly increased the percentage of apoptotic cells in T98G cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that knockdown of NMNAT, at the knockdown rate of 40–50% for NMNAT1 or at 20–30% for NMNAT2, significantly increased the percentage of apoptotic cells, including early apoptotic and late apoptotic cells (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: G2/M phase was only slightly increased in T98G cells with NMNAT1 knockdown.
source: The cell cycle assay showed G2/M phase was only slightly increased in T98G cells with NMNAT1 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: NMNAT promotes glioma cell growth mainly through inhibiting cell apoptosis.
source: These results suggest that NMNAT promotes glioma cell growth mainly through inhibiting cell apoptosis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the apoptosis and cell cycle data.

claim: Caspase-3 is the main effector protease cleaving a large number of substrates during apoptosis.
source: Caspase-3 is the main effector protease cleaving a large number of substrates during apoptosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about caspase-3 function.

claim: Nuclear translocation and accumulation of caspase-3 play a critical role in the progression of apoptosis.
source: Previous studies revealed that nuclear translocation and accumulation of caspase-3 play a critical role in the progression of apoptosis (Prokhorova et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Prokhorova et al., 2018.

claim: The caspase-mediated pathway is highly conserved in mammalian and Drosophila.
source: The caspase-mediated pathway is highly conserved in mammalian and Drosophila (Fuchs and Steller, 2011; Shi, 2001; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fuchs and Steller, 2011 and Shi, 2001, and illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Downregulation of DCP1 significantly increased glial neoplasia volume in Drosophila.
source: To validate the role of caspase pathway in Drosophila glial neoplasia, we examined tumor growth in flies with downregulation of DCP1, the homolog of mammalian caspase-3/7. In these flies, glial neoplasia volume was significantly increased (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting the important role of caspase-mediated apoptosis in preventing Drosophila glial neoplastic growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: There was a significant decrease of caspase-3 levels in glial neoplasms that overexpress Nmnat-PC (nuclear), compared with those overexpressing lacZ, Nmnat-PCWR (nuclear), or Nmnat-PD (cytoplasmic).
source: We used Repo and DAPI to label the nuclei region and observed a significant decrease of caspase-3 levels in glial neoplasms that overexpress Nmnat-PC (nuclear), compared with those overexpressing lacZ, Nmnat-PCWR (nuclear), or Nmnat-PD (cytoplasmic) (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and quantified in Figure 4C.

claim: When Nmnat was knocked down in Rasv12-expressing glial cells, significant nuclear enrichment of caspase-3 was observed.
source: In addition, when we knocked down Nmnat in Rasv12-expressing glial cells, we observed significant nuclear enrichment of caspase-3 (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B and quantified in Figure 4D.

claim: NMNAT is a negative regulator of glial neoplastic cell apoptosis in Drosophila.
source: These results suggest that NMNAT is a negative regulator of glial neoplastic cell apoptosis in Drosophila.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the caspase-3 localization and expression data.

claim: Knockdown of NMNAT led to increased nuclear caspase-3 in human glioma cells.
source: We found that knockdown of NMNAT led to increased nuclear caspase-3 (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and quantified in Figure 5C.

claim: Knockdown of NMNAT showed a specific increase of fully processed P17/19 species of cleaved caspase-3.
source: Western blot analysis showed a specific increase of fully processed P17/19 species of cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 5D), indicating the activation of apoptosis (Porter and Jänicke, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Overexpression of either NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 reduced nuclear caspase-3 in cisplatin-induced apoptosis.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of either NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 reduced nuclear caspase-3 in cisplatin-induced apoptosis (Figure 5B and E), specifically the fully processed cleaved caspase species P17/19 as shown by Western blot analysis (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B and quantified in Figure 5E, and Western blot data in Figure 5F.

claim: NMNAT promotes glioma growth by inhibiting caspase-mediated apoptosis.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that NMNAT promotes glioma growth by inhibiting caspase-mediated apoptosis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the caspase-3 expression and activation data in both Drosophila and human cells.

claim: A significant elevation of H2Av signal was observed in Nmnat-PC (nuclear) overexpressing brains compared to that in Nmnat-PD (cytoplasmic), Nmnat-PCWR (nuclear), or lacZ overexpressing brains.
source: We observed a significant elevation of H2Av signal in Nmnat-PC (nuclear) overexpressing brains compared to that in Nmnat-PD (cytoplasmic), Nmnat-PCWR (nuclear), or lacZ overexpressing brains (Figure 6A), suggesting DNA damage level is higher in glial neoplasia with Nmnat-PC (nuclear) overexpression.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A and quantified in Figure 6C.

claim: A significantly reduced nuclear p53 pool (~20%) was found in Nmnat-PC (nuclear) overexpressing glial neoplasia cells compared to control glial neoplasia cells (~40%).
source: We next examined the distribution of endogenous p53 in glial neoplasia and found that while in control glial neoplasia cells (LacZ group), p53 was relatively evenly distributed with ~40% of p53 in the nucleus, a significantly reduced nuclear p53 pool (~20%) was found in Nmnat-PC (nuclear) overexpressing glial neoplasia cells (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B and quantified in Figure 6D.

claim: Nmnat-PC (nuclear) expression potentially regulates p53 response to DNA damage to allow higher tolerance to DNA damage.
source: Together with the observation of higher DNA damage levels in Nmnat-PC (nuclear) overexpressing glial neoplasia cells, these results indicate that Nmnat-PC (nuclear) expression potentially regulates p53 response to DNA damage, presumably to allow higher tolerance to DNA damage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the DNA damage and p53 localization data.

claim: p53 is a key player controlling cell fate in response to DNA damage: initiate DNA repair when there is limited DNA damage, and induce apoptosis when DNA damage is too severe.
source: p53 is a key player controlling cell fate in response to DNA damage: initiate DNA repair when there is limited DNA damage, and induce apoptosis when DNA damage is too severe (Roos and Kaina, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Roos and Kaina, 2013.

claim: PFT-α is reported to inhibit translocation of p53 and affect p53-related transactivation.
source: PFT-α is reported to inhibit translocation of p53 and affect p53-related transactivation (Komarov et al., 1999; Leker et al., 2004; Murphy et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Komarov et al., 1999; Leker et al., 2004; Murphy et al., 2004.

claim: The glial neoplasia volume was significantly increased in PFT-α-treated flies compared to that in DMSO-treated flies.
source: The glial neoplasia volume was significantly increased in PFT-α-treated flies compared to that in DMSO-treated flies (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and quantified in Figure 7C.

claim: The increase in glial neoplasia volume with PFT-α treatment was accompanied by a decrease in survival.
source: The increase in glial neoplasia volume was accompanied by a decrease in survival (Figure 7B), and the reduced cleaved caspase-3 intensity (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PFT-α treatment reduced cleaved caspase-3 intensity in glial neoplasia.
source: The increase in glial neoplasia volume was accompanied by a decrease in survival (Figure 7B), and the reduced cleaved caspase-3 intensity (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A and quantified in Figure 7D.

claim: p53 is critical for inhibiting glial neoplastic growth in Drosophila.
source: These results suggest p53 is critical for inhibiting glial neoplastic growth in Drosophila, and p53 inhibition phenocopies NMNAT overexpression in glial neoplasia growth.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the p53 inhibitor treatment data.

claim: p53 inhibition phenocopies NMNAT overexpression in glial neoplasia growth.
source: These results suggest p53 is critical for inhibiting glial neoplastic growth in Drosophila, and p53 inhibition phenocopies NMNAT overexpression in glial neoplasia growth.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the effects of p53 inhibition and NMNAT overexpression.

claim: Cleaved caspase-3 expression level in p53 and NMNAT double knockdown cells was reduced compared to those in siNMNAT cells.
source: As shown in Figure 8 (shRNA lentiviral knockdown) and Figure 8—figure supplement 1 (siRNA knockdown), cleaved caspase-3 expression level in p53 and NMNAT double knockdown cells was reduced compared to those in siNMNAT cells, suggesting that p53 depletion reduced significantly cleaved caspase-3 expression in NMNAT knockdown glioma cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: p53 is a key mediator of NMNAT knockdown-induced apoptosis in glioma.
source: These results indicate p53 is a key mediator of NMNAT knockdown-induced apoptosis in glioma.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the p53 and NMNAT double knockdown experiments.

claim: PARP1 catalyzes NAD+-dependent PARylation of a large number of proteins (including p53) in response to DNA damage.
source: In response to DNA damage, PARP1 catalyzes NAD+-dependent PARylation of a large number of proteins (including p53), a process that is one of the largest NAD+ consumers in the nucleus (Fischbach et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fischbach et al., 2018 and Kim et al., 2005.

claim: PARylated p53 has reduced stability and activity.
source: It has been shown that PARylated p53 has reduced stability and activity (Simbulan-Rosenthal et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Simbulan-Rosenthal et al., 1999.

claim: Protein PARylation level was significantly increased in NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 overexpressing cells.
source: To test this hypothesis, we first examined the level of protein PARylation under NMNAT overexpression, and using dot blot analysis, we found that protein PARylation level was significantly increased in NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 overexpressing cells and significantly reduced with siRNA knockdown (Figure 9A and B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 9A-B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Protein PARylation level was significantly reduced with NMNAT siRNA knockdown.
source: To test this hypothesis, we first examined the level of protein PARylation under NMNAT overexpression, and using dot blot analysis, we found that protein PARylation level was significantly increased in NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 overexpressing cells and significantly reduced with siRNA knockdown (Figure 9A and B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: PARP1 and NMNAT proteins were detected in the p53-immunoprecipitated fraction.
source: Interestingly, we detected PARP1 and NMNAT proteins in the p53-immunoprecipitated fraction (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The level of PARP1 immunoprecipitated with p53 was increased with NMNAT overexpression.
source: Furthermore, although total p53 levels were not significantly affected by NMNAT expression, the level of PARP1 immunoprecipitated with p53 was increased with NMNAT overexpression (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: NMNAT interacts with p53 in U87MG cells.
source: We observed consistent results in U87MG cells that NMNAT interacts with p53 (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a presence of a trimeric p53/NMNAT/PARP1 complex.
source: These results suggest the presence of a trimeric p53/ NMNAT/PARP1 complex, and a potential role of NMNAT in promoting the trimeric complex formation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the immunoprecipitation and colocalization data.

claim: Colocalization of NMNAT1 with p53 was detected in T98G glioma cells expressing NMNAT1.
source: To confirm and extend the biochemical analysis, we carried out immunofluorescent colocalization studies of T98G glioma cells expressing NMNAT1 and detected the colocalization of NMNAT1 with p53 (Figure 9E1) as well as of NMNAT1 with PARP1 (Figure 9G1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9E1.

claim: Colocalization of NMNAT1 with PARP1 was detected in T98G glioma cells expressing NMNAT1.
source: To confirm and extend the biochemical analysis, we carried out immunofluorescent colocalization studies of T98G glioma cells expressing NMNAT1 and detected the colocalization of NMNAT1 with p53 (Figure 9E1) as well as of NMNAT1 with PARP1 (Figure 9G1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9G1.

claim: p53 protein level is not altered by NMNAT expression.
source: Consistent with Western blot analysis (Figure 9C), p53 protein level is not altered by NMNAT expression as p53 immunofluorescence intensity was similar between NMNAT1 expression cells and neighboring untransfected cells, or DsRed expressing control cells (Figure 9D2 and quantified in Figure 9H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9D2 and quantified in Figure 9H, and Western blot data in Figure 9C.

claim: The distribution of p53 changed from diffuse to clustered in NMNAT1-positive hotspots.
source: Interestingly, the distribution of p53 changed from diffuse to clustered in NMNAT1-positive hotspots, as visualized by a fluorescence surface plot in Figure 9E2'.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9E2'.

claim: PARP1 protein clustered in NMNAT1-positive hotspots.
source: Similarly, PARP1 protein also clustered in NMNAT1-positive hotspots (Figure 9G2 and G2'), suggesting the close proximity of NMNAT, p53, and PARP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9G2 and G2'.

claim: In NMNAT-expressing cells, PARP1 levels exhibit a small but significant upregulation.
source: In addition, in NMNAT-expressing cells, PARP1 levels exhibit a small but significant upregulation (Figure 9I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 9I.

claim: NMNAT interacts with PARP1 and promotes PARylation of PARP1-targeting proteins, including p53, through increasing the local NAD+ availability.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that NMNAT interacts with PARP1 and promotes PARylation of PARP1-targeting proteins, including p53, through increasing the local NAD+ availability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PARylation, immunoprecipitation, and colocalization data.

claim: p53 is acetylated by p300/CBP and deacetylated by SIRTs family of NAD+-dependent deacetylases.
source: In addition to PARylation, p53 is modified by another NAD+-dependent posttranslational modification (PTM), deacetylation. p53 is acetylated by p300/CBP and deacetylated by SIRTs family of NAD+-dependent deacetylases (Vaziri et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vaziri et al., 2001.

claim: SIRT1 is the major deacetylase regulating p53 activity through deacetylation of p53 at K382, and hence inhibiting the p53-mediated apoptosis pathway.
source: SIRT1 is the major deacetylase regulating p53 activity through deacetylation of p53 at K382, and hence inhibiting the p53-mediated apoptosis pathway (Cheng et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cheng et al., 2003.

claim: NMNAT1 has been reported to interact with SIRT1 directly.
source: NMNAT1 has been reported to interact with SIRT1 directly (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: With NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 overexpression, acetyl-p53 was specifically reduced while total p53 levels remained the same.
source: Interestingly, with NMNAT1 or NMNAT2 overexpression, acetyl-p53 was specifically reduced while total p53 levels remained the same (Figure 10A–C), although a stable complex of p53 and SIRT1 was not detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot data shown in Figure 10A-C.

claim: Endogenous SIRT1 expression was upregulated in NMNAT overexpressing cells.
source: It is interesting to note that endogenous SIRT1 expression was upregulated in NMNAT overexpressing cells (Figure 10D), suggesting a potential coregulation of NMNAT and SIRT1.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Similar results of reduced acetyl-p53 with NMNAT overexpression were observed in U87MG cells.
source: Notably, similar results were observed in U87MG cells (Figure 10—figure supplement 1), suggesting a common effect of NMNAT on p53 modification.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: NMNAT upregulation promotes the NAD+-dependent deacetylation of p53 and specifically reduces the pool of acetyl-p53.
source: Collectively, these results show that NMNAT upregulation promotes the NAD+-dependent deacetylation of p53 and specifically reduces the pool of acetyl-p53.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the acetyl-p53 and SIRT1 expression data.

claim: A strong negative correlation between NMNAT1 expression and survival can be seen in patients with brain lower grade glioma (LGG).
source: A strong negative correlation between NMNAT1 expression and survival can be seen in patients with brain lower grade glioma (LGG), with elevated NMNAT1 expression significantly associated with a lower disease-free survival rate, both when comparing survival in the median high-low tumor expression patient groups (Figure 11A) and in the highest and lowest 10% expression groups (Figure 11B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data from TCGA shown in Figure 11A and B.

claim: Elevated NMNAT1 expression is significantly associated with a lower disease-free survival rate in LGG patients.
source: A strong negative correlation between NMNAT1 expression and survival can be seen in patients with brain lower grade glioma (LGG), with elevated NMNAT1 expression significantly associated with a lower disease-free survival rate, both when comparing survival in the median high-low tumor expression patient groups (Figure 11A) and in the highest and lowest 10% expression groups (Figure 11B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data from TCGA shown in Figure 11A and B.

claim: High NMNAT1-expressing tumors (top 10%) in glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) showed a significant correlation with more aggressive disease and poorer outcome.
source: In the aggressive form of glioma, glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), from which the T98G and U87MG cell lines are derived, high NMNAT1-expressing tumors (top 10%) again showed a significant correlation with more aggressive disease and poorer outcome (Figure 11C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data from TCGA shown in Figure 11C.

claim: NMNAT2 GBM expression levels did not correlate with patient survival.
source: However, NMNAT2 GBM expression levels did not correlate with patient survival (Figure 11D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data from TCGA shown in Figure 11D.

claim: High NMNAT1 expression correlates with lower survival and poorer clinical outcome in brain glioma patients.
source: These brain glioma patient data set results indicate the strong correlation between high NMNAT1 expression with lower survival and poorer clinical outcome.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TCGA survival analysis data.

claim: PARylation and deacetylation modifications of p53 have been reported to inactivate p53-mediated function and activity.
source: As both PARylation and deacetylation modifications of p53 have been reported to inactivate p53-mediated function and activity (Juan et al., 2000; Luo et al., 2000; Malanga et al., 1998; Simbulan-Rosenthal et al., 1999), collectively, our results suggest a model where NMNAT promote glioma growth through facilitating NAD+-dependent PTMs of p53 to ameliorate apoptosis (Figure 11E).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Juan et al., 2000; Luo et al., 2000; Malanga et al., 1998; Simbulan-Rosenthal et al., 1999.

claim: NMNAT promotes glioma growth through facilitating NAD+-dependent PTMs of p53 to ameliorate apoptosis.
source: As both PARylation and deacetylation modifications of p53 have been reported to inactivate p53-mediated function and activity (Juan et al., 2000; Luo et al., 2000; Malanga et al., 1998; Simbulan-Rosenthal et al., 1999), collectively, our results suggest a model where NMNAT promote glioma growth through facilitating NAD+-dependent PTMs of p53 to ameliorate apoptosis (Figure 11E).
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.
